Adjusted operating income increased 130% to $424 million, representing a margin of 54%. Organic revenue growth was 3%. Growth trends across most of our businesses were broadly consistent with Q2. At AOL, the transition to advertising stack reduced its contribution to organic growth by approximately 1 percentage point relative to Q2. Growth at WeTransfer remained strong, both year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter, but a tougher comparable meant it contributed less to organic growth than in the prior quarter. I will now discuss progress across the three stages of our playbook: acquire, transform and optimize and reinvest.

According to recent reports, the first stage is acquire. During the quarter, we revealed the acquisitions of Airtable and Miro for a combined enterprise value of $2.65 billion. These acquisitions have now closed, and we have deployed Spooner teams to both, to build on the work done by the pre-acquisition teams. At Miro, we are currently focused on deepening our understanding of the business and developing our road map. At Airtable, we have announced our initial priorities and begun implementing them. These priorities are to improve the core offering, invest in AI and enable people and agents to collaborate with appropriate controls. Since acquisition, we have already shipped 60 product improvements.

We recently upgraded Omni, Airtable's built-in AI assistant and rolled out Canvas, which allows users to build custom apps on their data. Yesterday, we revealed the agreement to acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for an enterprise value of $3.68 billion. Mailchimp generated $1.27 billion in revenue in the 12 months to October 31 by helping customers proposal, execute and optimize their e-mail marketing campaigns. We see opportunities to improve the technology, product and monetization through our platform and are attracted by the business's scale and revenue predictability. The second stage of our playbook is transform and optimize. And for this call, I will focus on AOL, Eventbrite and Vimeo.

Based on the work done in Q3 and prior quarters, all 3 are positioned to accelerate growth in Q4. At AOL, planned subscription pricing and packaging adjustments were substantially completed by the end of Q3. By that point, most of the technological separation from Yahoo! was also behind us. Old desktop properties had migrated to a new instance of the advertising stack and mobile traffic has since transitioned. The disruption to advertising performance was broadly in line with expectations and the gap in impression pricing relative to Yahoo!'s stack had largely closed by mid-September. In October, we completed the rewrite of the iOS and Android apps, enabling us to start working on more significant product improvements.

Operating on our own technologies has enabled test across advertising and user experience with several experiments showing increases in engagement and advertising yield. At Eventbrite, we have shipped more than 70 product improvements in the 7 months since we acquired the business, and we continue to upgrade the business' technological infrastructure. Revenue also returned to year-over-year growth in October. Our primary focus has been on helping creators reach and better monetize larger audience, simplifying event management and improving technical reliability. Eventbrite events can now be discovered through ChatGPT and creators can automate ticket pricing changes using predefined rules. We have also strengthened waiting rooms to handle surges in ticket demand and introduced additional checks to combat bot purchases.

Alongside these improvements, we have introduced fresh monetization methods, including post-checkout advertising and a dedicated step for ticket add-ons. Turning to Vimeo. In Q3, bookings from both new and renewing customers grew year-over-year in each of the self-serve and enterprise segments. Trends in the OTT segment have been more challenging, but an overhauled checkout flow has lifted conversion for customers in early testing. Overall technical performance continues to improve, with medium video trans-coding volume decreasing by 40% between the start and the end of the quarter. New bookings per sales representative reached an all-time high in Q3 as we improved the team structure and invested in technology to support operations.

More recently, we introduced our free tier offering, unlimited storage for public videos, removing the previous 1 gigabyte cap. Alongside our commitments not to place advertising against uploaded videos or use them to train AI models, this offering is designed to make Vimeo a more attractive place for filmmakers to share their work. AOL, Eventbrite and Vimeo are still in their initial transformation phase, but we continue to improve our businesses well beyond the first year of ownership. For instance, in Q3, Meetup's revenue grew more than 20%, supported by Meetup+, the subscription offering for attendees.

It has been revealed that our objective is to compound per share earnings and free cash flow as rapidly as possible over the long term. We, therefore, assess each of our business primarily against our original return expectations. Remini has performed exceptionally well by this measure. Brightcove, after our somewhat disappointing start, has recently shown encouraging progress. Even with the benefit of hindsight, we would make both acquisitions again. We allocate Spooners where we see the most attractive prospective returns, and our platform enables us to regularly reallocate them as these opportunities evolve. During the quarter, we added over 80 net latest Spooners to our team, taking our core team to 753 full-time equivalents as of the end of Q3.

We have also continued to expand our use of AI to improve productivity. Today, 98% of our pull requests are written in full or in apart by AI. Since the start of the year, pull requests per Spooner software engineer have more than quadrupled while inference cost per pull request has roughly halved. These improvements reflect in part our investment in a proprietary harness to select models based on task requirements and inference cost. Beyond coding, we recently rolled out Diagram, a proprietary AI-powered design tool tailored to our workflows. With Diagram, every Spooner can develop a new user experience or slide deck from only a few natural language prompts, drastically reducing the design resources required.

We consider Diagram clearly better in our context than the third-party tools we were previously using. The third stage of our playbook is reinvest. As discussed last quarter, the pace at which we can reinvest and drive all 3 acquisitions is governed by three potential constraints: the availability of targets, our access to capital and our operational capacity. Hiring in AI are expanding our operational capacity. Those Spooners are currently our scarcest resource. Since the start of Q3, we have secured $8.35 billion in financing through debt and equity transactions and expanded revolving credit facilities.

Recent findings suggest that our debut bond issuance opened a new source of capital while the Berkshire Hathaway private placement and the placement announced yesterday have further strengthened our financial position. After deducting the funds expected to be used for the Mailchimp acquisition and upon closing of the placement, we have more than $4 billion of available liquidity to support further acquisitions. Enrico will now discuss our financial performance in more detail.

Enrico Martinelli: Thank you, Luca, and hello, everyone. For Q3, total revenue was $780 million, up 125%. Of this total, $38 million was attributable to Airtable, which was consolidated into our financials from September 4. Organic revenue growth was 3%. Similar to Q2, the strongest contributions to organic growth came from WeTransfer and Tractive. To provide some incremental detail the 2026 and 2025 acquisitions cohorts each grew revenue 6% year-over-year. The 2024 cohort, 8%; and the 2023 cohort, 10%. These figures reflect revenue-weighted growth and where applicable, include comparisons to pre-acquisition periods. This growth was partly offset by weakness at Remini, which reduced organic growth by 2 percentage points.

Recent findings suggest that we expect Remini to continue to face revenue pressure due to its historically relatively low retention rates, dependence on viral spikes for user acquisition and increased competition in the AI image generation market. So its impact on overall organic growth will be moderated by its declining size within our overall portfolio. Q3 operating income totaled $172 million, increasing 34%; and adjusted operating income reached $424 million, increasing 130%. Airtable contributed $10 million to adjusted operating income. Operating income as a percentage of revenue was 22%, down from 37% in Q3 '25. Adjusted operating income margin was 54%, expanding 1 percentage point compared to Q3 2025.

In a recent development, operating income as a percentage of revenue declined despite the improvement in adjusted operating income margin, primarily due to a $149 million increase in amortization of intangible assets. This increase reflected the businesses we acquired over the past year and the finalization of purchase price allocations for AOL, Eventbrite, Tractive and Vimeo. Finalizing these allocations resulted in a $65 million catch-up charge relating to prior periods. Transaction-related expense and other items not indicative of ongoing operating performance also pressured the operating income as a percentage of revenue, the former due to the acquisitions of Airtable and Miro and the latter due to the IPO-related costs.

The expansion in adjusted operating income margin was primarily driven by a 275 basis point decline in advertising expense as a percentage of revenue. This reduction is both a function of our strategy to select acquisition targets that are not highly reliant on paid advertising for user acquisition and the result of our work to eliminate inefficient expenditure. This improvement was partly offset by the impact of changes in portfolio mix on certain items within cost of revenue. IT infrastructure expense and other cost of revenue, both increased, while distribution and payment processing expense declined, all measured as a percentage of revenue. Together, these cost of revenue items reduced adjusted operating income margin by 125 basis points.

Interest expense was $107 million, rising 163% year-over-year, but broadly stable sequentially as outstanding debt in the quarter was consistent with Q2. Other expense was $17 million, primarily reflecting currency exchange losses, and we recognized an income tax benefit of $43 million. This benefit included the partial release of a valuation allowance associated with the finalized purchase price allocation for Vimeo. Diluted earnings per share was $0.13, down 3%; and adjusted earnings per share was $0.42, up 98%. Turning now to cash flow and our financial position. In Q3, net cash from operating activities totaled $261 million. We also received $1.09 billion in net proceeds from our IPO. We paid $1.21 billion for acquisitions, net of cash acquired.

Capital expenditure was $5 million. We also repaid $297 million under our revolving credit facilities and made $206 million in scheduled principal repayments of long-term debt. At quarter end, the carrying amount of long-term debt was $4.91 billion. Net debt fell by $187 million during the quarter to $4 billion at the end of Q3. Leverage ratio stood at 2.1x. Available liquidity totaled $3.36 billion, including cash and amounts available under committed term loan and revolving credit facilities. After quarter end, we paid $1.36 billion for Miro. We secured $4.46 billion from term loan add-ons, our first bond issuance, the Berkshire Hathaway private placement, the reinvestment by certain Miro shareholders and other borrowings.

These transaction amounts are gross of fees and associated costs. Given effect to these transactions, available liquidity at quarter end would have been $6.46 billion. The private placement announced yesterday would add $1.3 billion upon closing. The Mailchimp acquisition would reduce liquidity by $3.31 billion, net of Intuit's reinvestment. Had both pending transactions also closed at quarter end, available liquidity would have been $4.45 billion. Now to guidance. For Q4, we expect revenue to be in the range of $984 million to $1 billion. This represents organic revenue growth of 5% at the midpoint.

We expect adjusted operating income to be in the range of $470 million to $490 million, which represents an adjusted operating income margin of 48% at the midpoint. The implied sequential decline in this margin reflects the incorporation of the Airtable and Miro cost bases into our financials. We expect margins, excluding these businesses to expand both year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter. For the full financial year of 2026, this outlook implies revenue of between $3.07 billion and $3.09 billion, an increase from our prior guidance of $2.78 billion to $2.82 billion. It also implies full year 2026 adjusted operating income of $1.58 billion to $1.6 billion, an increase from the previously provided outlook of $1.46 billion to $1.51 billion.

In a recent development, both increases reflect a stronger outlook for businesses included in our prior guidance and contributions from Airtable and Miro. This guidance is based on the set of businesses we own today and doesn't incorporate any contribution from future acquisitions. Specifically, it includes a full quarter contribution from Airtable and Miro's contribution from October '26, but no contribution from the pending Mailchimp acquisition. With that, we are ready to start the Q&A portion of the call.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And now, we're going to take our first question, and the question comes from the line of Eric Sheridan from Goldman Sachs.

Eric Sheridan: Maybe 2, if I can. On the organic revenue piece, in terms of some of the acquired assets you have, once an acquired asset, maybe runs into either operational headwinds or slows from a growth perspective, how are you thinking about philosophically either reinvesting back in that business to stimulate organic revenue growth or optimize for margin or cash flow? And maybe if I could just ask a quick follow-up after that.

Industry observers note that luca Ferrari: This is Luca, Co-Founder, CEO. Thank you for the question. So our investment, whether it's R&D or sales and marketing is completely independent of organic revenue growth. We, at all times, ask ourselves the question of where that talent, that money would yield the highest possible returns and invest accordingly. So there could be a case where a business is declining and incremental investment would yield substantial uplift in free cash flows in the long run. We would -- assuming we have the resources, we would make that investment. In other cases, if we don't think we can influence that decline, we wouldn't. And the very same concept applies for a fast-growing business.

There are fast-growing businesses where growth, at least to the best of our knowledge, cannot be necessarily accelerated by further investments, at least not profitably and vice versa. And more generally, everything we do, whether at the individual business level and even more so when looking at Bending Spoons as a whole is aimed at compounding earnings and free cash flows per share as rapidly as possible with a multi-decade view. So organic revenue growth is not an indicator that really comes into play in those considerations.

Eric Sheridan: Great. And against the current capital markets environment, how is your view continuing to evolve in terms of the utilization of debt as opposed to the utilization of equity as either a source of capital or being issued in parallel to facilitating certain transactions on the M&A front?

Luca Ferrari: Thank you. Still me, still Luca. So basically, we start from the same objective of generating as much value in terms of earnings and free cash flows on a per share basis over the next 10 or 20 years and solve backward, and that applies to our financing as well. Now typically, if you look at our historical performance, we have delivered very high returns, I'd like to say, exceptional returns on our investments in acquisitions. And we have no reason right now to doubt that we'll continue to deliver outstanding returns going forward. So those returns have generally been substantially higher than the cost of our debt.

Industry observers note that and therefore, it's always been, in our view, wise to prioritize using debt as long as we kept our exposure at very prudent levels, which you could translate into a cap to leverage ratio, for example, and we assess this in a more sophisticated way internally. But as a rule of thumb, keeping leverage ratio in the 2 to 3 range, typically, we believe, results in a highly prudent posture. Of course, we reinvest all of our free cash flows into acquisitions because that's the highest return opportunity, at least it has been consistently so far, and we believe it will continue to be given just how rich our pipeline for acquisitions is.

Equity remains a very useful type of financing in -- when at least one of the following 2 criteria are met. Of course, the valuation needs to be decent enough that the cost of acquisition is not tremendous and in excess of our returns. But assuming valuation is in the range of acceptable, then it boils down to either it being useful to keep leverage ratio lower.

Industry observers note that we naturally delever pretty promptly, but sometimes we want to lower it faster than we would by simply operating the business or, and it's really 2 phases of the same coin, to be able to go after a larger target that we couldn't really reach not in the short term through the investment of our free cash flows and incremental debt alone. So we always redeploy free cash flows. We always raise incremental debt while keeping leverage at prudent levels.

And then time and again, we might go back to the equity markets if we think that doing so helps either further improve our risk profile or grow faster on a per share basis, which is what you have seen recently. While the IPO naturally, we had to problem equity to get it done, and that helps with access to the debt markets, too. But after that, we raised a little bit of money from Berkshire Hathaway. Yesterday, we unveiled a PIPE for another $1.3 billion. And a couple of the recent acquisitions, the seller reinvested a small percentage of the overall consideration into newly issued Bending Spoons stock.

So we are not shy when it comes to using equity as long as we believe that, that helps us compound value for our shareholders even faster.

Operator: Now we're going to take our next question, and it comes from the line of Kirk Materne from Evercore ISI.

Kirk Materne: With Airtable, Miro and now Mailchimp, you all are definitely moving further into enterprise-oriented businesses. Can you just talk about how the way you apply the Bending Spoons playbook maybe changes a little bit as you go into enterprise versus what's worked in consumer. They have longer customer relationships, implementation sales motions. I'm just kind of curious how you guys think about that. It might be more nuanced than anything more dramatic, but I'd love to just hear your thoughts on that as you've now done 3 in a row in that area?

Recent findings suggest that luca Ferrari: Thank you. So I would say Mailchimp actually, I wouldn't call it enterprise, although it serves I believe, about 1 million customers. So there's a little bit of everything in there, but primarily, it's, let's say, SMEs, and it's almost fully self-serve. So there is -- the sales motion is very limited, almost nonexistent at the scale of the entire business. And so it's actually closer to our more typical acquisitions from the past than Airtable and Miro, both of which have primarily enterprise customers and a sales-led go-to-market motion.

Recent findings suggest that now what we have found over time is that the biggest differences in customer behavior and optimal tactics and approaches are driven by whether a business is primarily self-serve versus sales-led and not so much whether it's consumer or B2B. We find that self-serve consumer behaves actually quite similarly to self-serve, let say, SMEs, whereas the big differences come when you switch from self-serve to having to deal with customers through human beings and negotiations and procurement departments.

Recent findings suggest that both can be optimized in very -- in excellent ways, but they require different skill set, different approaches and to some extent, different underlying technologies, which is why, by the way, precisely to approach perfection in sales-led enterprise we have invested quite aggressively, particularly this year in developing not just insights and expertise, but also underlying proprietary tooling. We developed -- we created a dedicated team of engineers and product managers and they have been hard at work to create tools that make our salespeople more efficient. We had some excellent results better than at least personally, I expected. For example, at Vimeo, we managed to achieve the highest level of new bookings per salesperson in Vimeo's history.

And this is important because Vimeo clearly is not in an up-and-coming explosive growth kind of phase where that would happen naturally, quite the opposite, right? And that was achieved at the same time as we actually got to the maximum level of absolute newly introduced bookings. So this is not the product of a shrinkage in the sales force where we only kept the highest performing salespeople. Naturally, the proprietary technologies we put to work are not the only reason. There's a lot of work on organization and processes and the approach.

But it is reassuring and encouraging as we keep working on becoming really good at this as I believe we have proven to be at the self-serve side of the equation.

Operator: Now we're going to take our next question. And the question comes from the line of Alec Brondolo from Wells Fargo.

Alec Brondolo: Perhaps 2 for me. First, on AOL. As you noted in the prepared remarks, there was a price increase taken during the quarter. Could you just speak to how the user base responded to that price increase, the level of churn, if any, relative to your expectations? And then secondly, with regards to the 5% organic revenue growth guidance in the fourth quarter, could you perhaps just unpack that a little bit? I think that Airtable and Miro are going to be included in that. They're obviously growing a little bit faster. So how much of that acceleration -- sequential acceleration is the inclusion of Airtable and Miro relative to the rest of the portfolio improving?

Luca Ferrari: Thank you. So yes, AOL, like every one of our businesses, we experimented extensively with all sorts of monetization changes well beyond mere pricing, but pricing being one of the things. We have done this the entire time since the acquisition closed in January. And we have identified several changes in configurations that based on our testing, yield substantial improvements in revenue trajectory. We did begin deploying one of these configurations at scale recently with high expectations given our extensive testing of nice revenue uplift, modest one-off churn and no impact on, let's say, long-term ongoing churn levels.

So the expected result is to see an improvement in revenue levels at no cost in terms of revenue quality after the short-lived transitional period where, of course, churn spikes a little bit. We've really just very recently deployed that at scale. So the impact of that applies almost not at all in Q3, although very slightly does, and it will apply from Q4 and onward for most of 2027 as well. That's our expectation. Now regarding the Q4 5 percentage points in organic growth at the midpoint of the range, we expect most of our businesses to continue performing along similar lines.

The main changes sequentially vis-a-vis Q3 would be we expect AOL, Eventbrite and Vimeo to each do better than their past trajectories. So those would have a nice impact there, I think more so AOL and Vimeo. At Eventbrite, we have not touched prices or almost -- monetization almost at all with the exception of a little bit of advertising work. And so we expect growth to be a little bit slower, but still positive, which is newly introduced after a couple of years of declines for Eventbrite. So I believe an excellent result. We'll be able to report more on that in the next couple of quarters as all the numbers come in, but we're quite positively impressed.

And so again, AOL and Vimeo will probably do most of the heavy lifting vis-a-vis Q3 and then, of course, being able to account for both Airtable and Miro for the full quarter will help. We think they will contribute approximately 1 percentage point to guidance.

Operator: Now we're going to take our next question. And the question comes from the line of Omar Dessouky from Bank of America.

For example, like what percentage of payers don't use the apps on a monthly basis? And have you recently seen any uptick in the pace of cancellations? And the second part of the question is, would you say your consumer subscriptions will be unaffected or experience limited impact as a result of AI agents informing the consumers of their subscription inventory?

Industry observers note that luca Ferrari: Thank you for the question. I've not seen the videos, but of course, I understand the concept you're describing. So I think it's a reasonable concern for an investor to have. I would certainly recommend people to embed a little bit of a buffer for adverse events in general, and this could be one of those. Now I'll give you a number of facts that I believe seem to indicate this to be a reason for very limited concern. First of all, only about 1/3 of our revenues from consumer subscriptions.

According to recent reports, second of all, we actually looked very closely last week in anticipating the question, product by product, and we could not find even the slightest impact on any key indicator, whether it's gross retention, net retention and any other indicator of business health across the entire portfolio. So, so far, we feel very confident saying 0 impact whatsoever. It's also worth noting that products meant to help customers manage their subscriptions, including canceling subscriptions they are presumably not using that have been introduced. I remember at least 2 separate such products being launched by startups over the past 5 or 6 years. I never followed closely.

But to my knowledge, they never saw any commercial success, which I think indicates that probably consumers in general, they don't think they have this problem. I mean I'm sure there's 10 billion people out there. So certainly someone does. But that, to me, seems to indicate that this is not something people feel they need help with. It's also worth noting that I can only speak when it comes to this about our products, but we make notifications and cancellations extremely easy. So we notify our customers on their payments. And of course, credit card providers do so, and you can find it on your bank account summary.

And we make cancellation extremely easy, generally a couple of clicks across most of our products, at least after we've owned them for a while. Sometimes when we buy them, previous owners were not as thoughtful and customer-friendly, but we always make sure to transition to very friendly cancellation procedures within the first year or so. So it's -- at least for our product, it's very hard to believe people would find that it's difficult to cancel. They can also contact customer support. They just need to say, I want to cancel and we basically cancel, no questions asked.

It has been revealed that and last but not least, we try pretty hard to make sure our products are great and worth using and paying for. And they're certainly not perfect, but I believe they're in almost every case, very, very good, and we try to make them better by the day. So is this a potential risk? I would say I would be responsible if I said it's impossible this ever impacts Bending Spoons. Based on what we see and all these factual considerations, we find it hard to believe this would be a major headwind at some point, although it's reasonable to expect that at some point, in at least some cases, we may see a little bit of deterioration.

It has been revealed that and when that happens, we'll let you know. But again, so far, absolutely no signal whatsoever.

Operator: And now, we'll take our next question, and it comes from the line of Bryan Smilek from JPMorgan.

Recent findings suggest that bryan Smilek: Luca, curious, can you just help us better understand the ad road map at Eventbrite across post checkout and first-party ad revenue more broadly? I guess like how do you think about modulating ad load over time and the potential subscription opportunity in a more meaningful way at Eventbrite?

Luca Ferrari: Thank you for the question. So I'm a little bit wary of stealing the team's thunder when it comes -- like we like our teams to give them a lot of autonomy and be able to communicate and announce their own plans and achievements. But what I can say is that we see a significant opportunity at Eventbrite on both advertising and subscriptions monetization. For example, we recently introduced post-checkout ads. And for those of you who have not used Eventbrite or maybe are not as well versed with the sort of things, it means that after a potential attendee purchases a ticket, there is, of course, a page there for summary.

We now display advertising, and that's led to a nice uplift in advertising revenue, had absolutely no impact on engagement or retention or any other metric you want to keep healthy. We have also helped -- and this is part of advertising, but slightly different. We've also helped event organizers advertise more and more effectively on Eventbrite because as an event organizer, you may want to spend a little bit of money to make sure your event is more prominently displayed on the platform. We have 80 million people come to Eventbrite every month to look for things to do.

According to recent reports, and so being more prominently displayed can make a huge difference in how many tickets you sell and often lead to a good return on investment. And so we made some changes there to the user experience for our event organizers, and that led to a very noticeable uplift in how much they spend, and we believe it's also good for them based on what we've been able to see so far.

So that also so far has been successful, and we believe it's only the beginning of things we can do to improve that offering, not just its presentation, but substantially the value it can deliver also by adding sophistication in how we -- in what events we show to whom. And so we want to make that advertising investment more and more accretive for our event organizers. When it comes to subscriptions, we have introduced 2 different subscription -- well, it's really multiple versions really because we tested a huge variety of things. But to keep it relatively simple, we tested 2 types of subscriptions, one for consumers for attendees and one for the organizers themselves.

For the attendees, they now have the possibility of purchasing an ongoing subscription to -- so that all fees by Eventbrite are waived for their ticket purchases. And this is interesting for people who purchase frequently on Eventbrite. We have consumers who go to multiple events each month, and this is a good deal for them. And this is showing nice penetration and retention. And again, it has had so far in all of our experiments, no detrimental impact on all the things you care about, such as engagement and retention and satisfaction of attendees. And the one for organizers instead offers advanced marketing features.

According to recent reports, in particular, it offers e-mail marketing automations, which is funny because now we unveiled the acquisition of Mailchimp, but I promise we started this before we knew that was a possibility. And also, it enables SMS campaigns, which is something that wasn't available before. And so far, reception by organizers has been very positive because it doesn't -- these are not necessary tools. So the subscription is perceived to be in no way intrusive or limiting of what they can do on the platform if they want to be, let's say, less sophisticated or ambitious with their events.

But for those who want to try to go a little bit further, then it can be pretty good value for money based on what we've seen so far. And all of these areas, we think, are just scratching the surface. And hopefully, over the next multiple years, we can bring our offering to the next level.

Operator: Now we're going to take our next question, and the question comes from the line of Stefan Slowinski from BNP Paribas.

According to recent reports, stefan Slowinski: I've got 2. First one is on Mailchimp more specifically. I just wanted to double-click on that acquisition. We've seen over the past few years Intuit, first, investing a lot in the product and trying to get the product right and then more recently, significant cost cutting to shift to more of a kind of cash strategy for the company. So it's a business that's already seen a lot of product investment and cost cutting. And so just wondering kind of what gives you the confidence that you can get the returns that you need from that business? Where do you see the opportunity?

According to recent reports, and why are you paying maybe slightly above the 2.5x revenues that maybe you paid for previous acquisitions? That's the first question.

According to recent reports, luca Ferrari: Thank you. It's a wise observation. So just a quick accuracy pointer. So historically, we have paid anywhere between -- in most cases, anywhere between 1 and 6x revenue for our acquisitions. So it's really a pretty wide range. And yes, if you -- I believe if you average for acquisitions 2023 through 2025, it's probably like 2.5x. But if you shift that window, it can easily fluctuate, easily by a point or so. So this is -- it's true.

This is close to that average, but a little bit above our more recent range, partly because we think as we scale -- as we have talked about multiple times before, as we scale, it's reasonable to expect returns to moderate a little bit. Now they have been absolutely astronomical in the past. We have no reason to think that there will be anything less than outstanding going forward. But even then, it's reasonable to expect a little bit of compression. And this could be -- it's hard to tell whether this is a trend or just one deal, but we do expect slightly inferior returns from this deal than some other deals, but still amazing.

I mean, returns, I think most companies would feel for, to be clear. Now -- specifically to, let's say, product investment and then cost reduction, a lot of the acquisitions we have done in the past, you could argue similar things. When we bought Evernote, there had been a tremendous amount of investment in the product. And yet I believe we -- demonstrably, if you look at what we have done over the past few years, we managed to bring it to a whole new level. I think even the people who hate us for having increased prices would generally agree that the product has improved by leaps and bounds.

According to recent reports, and so -- and I could go on and on and most of our acquisitions were -- had been in both phases or at least one of those phases, and that has not prevented us from doing better. We have no reason to believe that we will not be able to improve performance at Mailchimp substantially going forward or else we wouldn't have offered this price. We're very excited about the acquisition. We see substantial opportunity to improve both revenue and cost. And we also like a few other things about it. First, of course, the scale. We talked about it in the past.

One disadvantage of our model is that those integrations, which are as deep as it gets technologically, people-wise, and those transformations, which also are sometimes dramatic, they take a lot of operational effort, and we don't have an infinite number of people. But thankfully, we find that the number of tuners we need to deploy to take care of those things does not scale anywhere linearly with revenue potential of an acquisition. And so larger scale acquisitions are much preferable. So of course, Mailchimp checks that box with flying colors. We believe it's -- the earnings will be predictable because this is such a long-standing business. We have a couple of decades' worth of data.

We've been able to study cohort behavior across all sorts of situations. COVID, of course, for digital business is super relevant , situations where competition intensified tremendously. Now the market has been relatively stable for quite a few years, but there was a period after Mailchimp really a trailblazer in e-mail marketing automation that a lot of competitors joined and many had plenty of financing and we were aggressive on marketing. #16264. Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are All Over It

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2201 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are All Over It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2201 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.
  • But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto.
  • It has been revealed that something must be behind all of this, you might think—a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.

Microsoft Outlook? Broken, for a bit. Air traffic control? Had some complications. Bank with Chase? Monday was not great. But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto. I am almost certainly forgetting some.

It has been revealed that something must be behind all of this, you might think—a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet? But the answer is more complicated than that. All of these problems, and the ones that will happen after I write this, are probably unconnected, at least in the concrete sense. But they exist in a world where the infrastructure of the internet and the whole human world it undergirds looks increasingly precarious.

Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, called last month “Black October.” This month? “Blacker November.” December probably isn’t looking great.

“This is not getting better, unfortunately,” Meyers told me.

One significant reason for all of this, although not the only one, is artificial intelligence, but maybe not in the ways you expect.

It has been revealed that if it’s connected to the internet, it’s at risk. Websites, sure. But also utilities like power plants and water treatment facilities or, for some reason, grocery store freezers.

In the olden days, like six months ago, a hacker taking control would have required a fairly complicated set of skills, honed over a long career, perhaps in the employ of a government or criminal organization.

Artificial intelligence, especially models developed and released this year, has changed things. AI has “democratized” hacking, cybersecurity experts told me. Things that used to require the capabilities and focus of a team of people with a clear goal can be done by a 20-something with an AI model and a specially designed program around it. And you don’t have to be a big or valuable target anymore to be worthy of a hacker’s attention.

It has been revealed that at the same time, AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities. These models and agents — essentially AI models that can do things on their own — can comb through websites or code and find problems that might have escaped the notice of humans. And they can do so more cheaply, meaning they can be turned on code that might not otherwise have gotten a close look. So many vulnerabilities are being exposed that it’s been given an appropriately bleak name: the vulnpocalypse.

Sources indicate that even that defensive advantage is a double-edged sword. Before, it might have taken weeks before a newly discovered vulnerability could be exploited. Now it might take days, even hours. If you’re responsible for a website or any of those things connected to the internet that may or may not still be maintained by their creators, you may not be paying attention and know you should enhancement. You may find yourself liable if a breach leads to a leak of customer data. You may not have the know-how to fix it.

Another risk introduced by AI is that the technology, trained on all the lines of code its creators could find, is really good at writing code. Software engineers know this, and companies are now maintaining smaller teams of human engineers using AI to write more and more software. That code might be OK, but it might not be, and there’s a chance no human ever looked at it to be sure.

In a recent development, when I connected with John Strand over video chat, he was in Germany for a conference, and he was smiling. That wasn’t good. “You need to understand that whenever an offensive security person smiles and gets excited,” he said, “it’s bad.”.

As owner and CEO of Black Hills Information Security, Strand’s job is to test systems for weaknesses, to think like an attacker and poke holes in a client’s defenses. He states he’d been getting a bit bored with the work after decades of the same techniques until the cyber capabilities of AI models started to explode at the end of 2025. Newly introduced AI models were great at finding weaknesses in code, and AI agents could do the boring, time-consuming part.

“You’re seeing something that can automate the kind of grinding grunt work of offensive security and bring that to a human operator much faster,” Strand remarked.

Things have only accelerated since the summer. AI agents are capable of more autonomy. And attackers have better tools to refine the often blunt instruments of AI models — harnesses. While an AI model can do a lot of things, a harness provides the tools and direction that allow it to do a specific thing more effectively. Think Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s Codex, but for hacking. Perhaps the biggest, most notable harness used by hackers is Artex, a significant-enough threat that the FBI issued a warning last week.

In a recent development, in September and October, a hack of major South Korean banks led to the theft of personal information. Meyers indicates CrowdStrike determined the attacker was likely a 26-year-old in China using Artex. After asking AI how to do the attack, the hacker succeeded, then asked the AI how to sell the stolen data on Telegram.

“Anybody out there can now be a nation-state-level hacker just by using the tool,” Meyers said.

According to recent reports, despite efforts by major AI developers to limit who can access their biggest and most capable models, the hacking and exploit skills attackers need are within the means of models already in the hands of attackers. That includes open-weight models that hackers can run on their own hardware, away from the guardrails and peering eyes of AI companies and government agencies.

“The genie’s out of the bottle, and there’s no putting it back in,” mentioned Gary Barlet, public sector chief technology officer at Illumio, a firm that specializes in ransomware and breach containment.

In a recent development, AI-powered hackers, whether they’re individual vibe-hackers or government-backed cyberwarfare units intent on damaging critical infrastructure, always have an advantage. They just have to be right once, as the saying goes. Defenders have to be right every time.

The good thing is that the defenders are using the same tools as the attackers. And sometimes they have a head start. Programs like Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, OpenAI’s Daybreak and Google’s Fairwind let cybersecurity experts and high-profile targets like banks and healthcare providers have early access to the most capable models from those developers, often with fewer limits on what the models can find. The goal is to get a jump on patching and fixing the easiest and riskiest problems.

It still might not be enough, and Significant Tech leaders know it. In an October appearance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stated he no longer thought we’d be able to “just patch all the bugs” and that the problem is one that “is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders or countries or individuals, taken seriously.”.

And defenders may not have much of a lead in patching bugs anyway, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week at the Upcoming York Times Dealbook Summit. Previously, when patching a critical system, you might have a week to test it before pushing it to production. “Right now the patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild,” Nadella said. “That’s going to create instability.”.

The PHP vulnerability widely reported in October — with an urgent notice from the PHP Foundation for website owners to patch — stemmed from work through Patch the Planet, part of OpenAI’s Daybreak.

That’s just one high-profile recent disclosure. But there has been an avalanche of them. The National Vulnerability Database has received more than 10,000 instances of common vulnerabilities and exposures so far in November, after more than 17,000 CVEs in October. For comparison, in October 2025, that figure was less than 5,000.

“There’s effectively this major backlog of security issues in the open-source world that hadn’t been discovered until AI was able to just spend tons of time analyzing it and finding these vulnerabilities,” remarked Matt Wyckhouse, CEO of Finite State, a cybersecurity company focused on connected devices.

Sources indicate that it goes well beyond open-source software. The connected devices Wyckhouse focuses on include things like refrigerators and smart home gadgets — the kinds of things that probably didn’t have to be connected to the internet, but are. The source code of the firmware and software powering those products has been seen by far fewer eyes than something like PHP, an incredibly common coding language used by much of the internet. The code running these devices may not be on GitHub or floating around the internet, but an AI model might be able to reverse-engineer it and find an exploit. And suddenly an attacker can turn freezers into ovens. If you think ground beef is expensive now, imagine what would happen if a major retailer’s stock of hamburger all spoiled overnight.

“Refrigeration has to work for our society to function, as it turns out,” Wyckhouse said.

It has been revealed that wherever the vulnerability is found, it has to be patched. That’s where the backlog of complications is really wreaking havoc. Companies that create or just operate software are swamped with vital, critical issues that have to be fixed now because it could only be hours before an attacker can exploit it. It’s why your computer and the software on it have to update so frequently these days.

“It’s daunting the amount of work and the amount of time it’s going to take to clean this whole thing up,” remarked Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov.

Industry observers note that and patching isn’t perfect. Sometimes it’s not a cyberattack that causes a system to go down but the fix to prevent it. Software updates are believed to be responsible for several of the recent high-profile outages, including Apple’s issues on Tuesday.

Things get even hairier if the code isn’t great to begin with or presents new problems of its own. And with AI writing even more of it, that’s a growing matter.

In the backdrop of all of this chaos is the fact that software engineering is one of the industries most disrupted by AI. Models trained on miles of code are great at writing something that works — no matter how many holes are in it. And to CEOs eager to cut costs and boost their companies’ stock prices, the temptation is to lay off engineers and have fewer people use AI to do all that coding.

Massive Tech has been laying off staff by the thousands this year. Microsoft’s October announcement that it was offering buyouts to 60,000 staff became a key talking point just weeks later when the system powering its Outlook email service went dark for a day. Might things break less often if more people were on hand to maintain them?

“I wouldn’t be surprised if companies start to backtrack on that more,” remarked Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at the database security firm Liquibase.

Companies might also have more junior developers writing and releasing code that would have previously gone through senior developers, with AI replacing the productivity, but not the experience, McCurdy notes.

That means the problem isn’t just the vulnerabilities in existing software, but the vulnerabilities being written into upcoming software or patches to existing software by AI. The same technology is causing the problem, providing the solution and complicating that solution.

The main thing we can do now is just… wait. Wyckhouse told me he thinks the next two years are going to be a period of growing pains as vulnerabilities are found and patched. The end result should be that everything is more stable.

“I think software is going to be an order of magnitude more secure by the end of the next year or two than it is today for this reason,” he remarked. “It will hurt a bit.”.

Whether you’re an ordinary phone user or a major corporation, updating your software has become more important than ever.

“You’ve got to patch. You go for a flu shot, and you go and have your preventative healthcare,” Meyers said. “You need to do the same thing when it comes to cybersecurity.”.

But consumers aren’t without power, especially when it comes to data breaches. If a tech giant isn’t properly maintaining its systems and protecting your privacy or security online, don’t use it. Having your data hacked and compromised has become ordinary. We get letters in the mail saying someone stole data from our bank or doctor’s office, and if we jump through the following hoops, we can get 12 months of identity protection.

We don’t have to put up with it, Barlet indicates. “I think we need to start having higher expectations from the companies we’re consuming from,” he mentioned.

Tech Report: Meta Muse booked an Airbnb without permission – and that’s not the worst of it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta’s Muse AI agent has only been around for a few months, but already has a track record of user privacy violations.
  • In a recent development, also: Don’t use Muse?
  • According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse stated the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta’s Muse AI agent has only been around for a few months, but already has a track record of user privacy violations. Even Meta employees are reporting concerning incidents, including the agent taking actions they didn’t ask it to and sharing information they didn’t recognize that appears to belong to other users.

In a recent development, also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages.

According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse stated the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.

These incidents “prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data,” Reuters mentioned.

Reuters said “an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: ‘BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2,722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5,899.57.'” In another instance, Muse booked a non-refundable Airbnb for an employee who hadn’t instructed it to.

Muse notified another employee, who was using the agent on her personal phone, about a message she’d received on Signal, though she said she hadn’t given the agent access to the encrypted messaging app.

Also: Meta Muse is the worst AI agent for privacy – and I’ve tried them all.

Reuters and the AI Now Institute determined, through testing on an Android phone and a Mac, that Muse used “permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.” Because Muse is set up with automatic access to Android push notifications, it didn’t need explicit app access to read messages.

The tests did not work on an iPhone, suggesting better protections against Muse’s prying.

Recent findings suggest that similarly, in September, a user reported Muse had shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before checking with him. The incident was ultimately a misunderstanding between the terms the user thought he’d consented to and how much access he was actually handing over, which exemplifies that Meta and the user may have explicitly different definitions of access, and that Muse can take advantage of that grey area.

Meta told Reuters these incidents were either isolated or the result of hallucinations, though Reuters could not confirm that.

These are just the latest in a string of alarming incidents surrounding Muse. In its first month, a cybersecurity professional discovered Muse had a serious zero-day bug that made it hijackable. At least one journalist found the AI sifting through his Apple Messages after he’d explicitly denied those permissions, which Apple then issued stronger privacy protections to address. Banks have also blocked agents over concerns.

As a firm, Meta doesn’t have a solid history of respecting user privacy. That legacy is partly what informed ZDNET contributor David Gewirtz’s suspicion of the AI assistant when he tested it, though it earned his assigned title of “worst AI agent for privacy” all on its own. The agent asked him for everything from contacts and chats to his logins and passwords, and Meta automatically uses conversations with Muse to train its AI.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac.

It has been revealed that public awareness of the risks of AI agents hit a peak last year with the viral OpenClaw. The predominant advice for using agents has been to take every privacy precaution: Be careful with the data you share and the apps you give it permissions for, and watch what you tell it. But if owners believe they’re doing so by restricting access to certain apps, just for Muse to find a way in anyway, privacy hygiene isn’t enough.

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible.

Reuters’ findings may provide an opportunity for Google’s agentic offering, now called Tasks (formerly Spark), which it made free (with usage limits, like Muse) this week.

I Didn’t Know Southwest Points Could Be This Valuable

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in a world of transferable points currencies, you might not think holding an airline or hotel credit card is necessary.
  • Industry observers note that take Southwest Airlines, for example.
  • Sources indicate that "Experiences create lifetime memories,” claims Nandika Suri, Southwest’s vice president of Rapid Rewards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in a world of transferable points currencies, you might not think holding an airline or hotel credit card is necessary. But travel brands are pushing back against that narrative, offering exclusive perks and redemption packages to those who carry their cards.

Industry observers note that take Southwest Airlines, for example. Its Rapid Rewards loyalty program allows you to redeem points for flights, but it also offers a special program called Rapid Rewards Access Events exclusively for Southwest credit cardholders. In exchange for a decent chunk of points, you can get a vacation package that’s worth significantly more than the price you pay. Instead of a traditional flight award redemption, you get a cohesive travel experience.

Sources indicate that "Experiences create lifetime memories,” claims Nandika Suri, Southwest’s vice president of Rapid Rewards. “For us, we really want them to have great memories and remember our brand as part of that.”.

Southwest invited me to participate in one of its Rapid Rewards Access Events. While Southwest covered the cost of my trip, these opinions are my own. Here’s what I learned.

Every event is different (ranging from concerts to multiday trips), but big-ticket Rapid Rewards Access Events tend to include flights, hotel accommodations, meals and excursions.

According to recent reports, the event I participated in was in Maui to celebrate the 30th anniversary of Southwest and Chase’s partnership. This was a bigger production than the typical event, with about 60 cardholders (and a plus one) participating. A typical multiday event might have 20 or 25 packages for sale.

In exchange for 275,000 Rapid Rewards points, cardholders received for themselves and one guest:.

A four-night stay in an ocean-view room at the Grand Wailea, a Waldorf Astoria Resort, in Maui, including daily breakfast.

Ground transportation between the airport and the resort, as well as for any scheduled group activities.

A special welcome reception and farewell dinner.

A snorkeling cruise with lunch and beverages included.

A choice between several excursions, including a spa treatment, golf, ziplining and more.

According to recent reports, even at extremely conservative estimates, I would value all of those things at roughly $4,600. That’s $750 more than what NerdWallet values 275,000 Rapid Rewards points at, according to our 2026 data. If we took a more liberal approach, I think it would be fair to say the package was worth more than $7,000. That puts this redemption between 1.7 and 2.5 cents per point. (Expand the section below to see how I arrived at those numbers.).

As of 2026, NerdWallet values Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.4 cents apiece. That puts the 275,000-point Southwest event package at $3,850.

Let’s put some numbers to the package inclusions and see how the points price stacks up to the cash valuation.

$1,000 Southwest gift card: It’s pretty easy to value a $1,000 Southwest gift card at $1,000. You need to fly to the event, so that can be taken at face value. (You could also use it toward a different trip, if you wanted to use points or fly with a different carrier.).

Four-night hotel stay: For the Grand Wailea stay, a nonrefundable Hilton Honors discount rate for an ocean-view room on the exact same dates in 2027 costs $4,490.19, after factoring in taxes and fees. (The base-level terrace-view room would cost $3,992.17.).

Sources indicate that if you were to use points, a standard room without an ocean view would cost 130,000 Hilton points per night. An ocean-view room’s rate shoots up to 281,000 Hilton points per night.

Using NerdWallet’s 2026 valuation of Hilton points at 0.4 cent per point, that puts the value of the two rooms at $2,080 and $4,496, respectively. To make things interesting, let’s say the hotel stay is worth $2,080.

In a recent development, daily breakfast at the hotel buffet is about $60 per person, before tax and tip. For four days, let’s put that at around another $500, bringing the total stay value to $2,580.

Ground transportation: Let’s make things simple and just say it’s $30 each way between the airport and the resort. For two people, that would be worth $120.

Welcome reception and farewell dinner: Southwest and Chase put a lot of effort into making these events nice, from the food and free-flowing alcohol to the entertainment (there was even a fire performance at the farewell dinner).

I would value this at $50 per person, conservatively, or $200 total.

Snorkeling cruise: I went on Viator to find a similar experience, and the cheapest option I found was priced at $100 per person.

Recent findings suggest that again, let’s price it conservatively and say it’s worth $200. That price doesn't include hotel transportation, gratuities, towels or alcoholic beverages, while the Southwest package did.

Excursion choice: Southwest let everyone choose an excursion, ranging from a chill pool or spa day to ziplining through the jungle or learning to surf.

It’s hard to put a number on this, because the activities varied in cost.

It has been revealed that I went ziplining, and it was $240 for six lines. That price doesn’t include transportation to the excursion, which was covered by Southwest. Meanwhile, a standard massage at the hotel spa is $275 (and that doesn’t even factor in the 20% service charge).

Let’s put this at $250 per person, giving us a round $500 for two people’s excursions.

It has been revealed that grand total: Summing up these numbers gets us $4,600. That’s $750 more than the $3,850 NerdWallet values 275,000 points at, but keep in mind that we probably undervalued several of the inclusions. The actual value of a trip like this could be much higher.

It also doesn’t factor in other things, like snacks provided at the hospitality booth, as well as surprise gifts and goodie bags prepared by Southwest and Chase for attendees.

Before you book a Rapid Rewards Access Event, there are some drawbacks to booking a vacation this way.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest one is if you don’t like group trips or following a schedule on your vacations. Given the nature of these events, you’ll be surrounded by a group of travelers, many of whom will likely be longtime Southwest flyers. If you prefer to keep to yourself, then this type of trip is likely not a good fit.

In a recent development, you’ll also have multiple scheduled activities on your itinerary. While you can choose to not show up, those activities add a lot of value to the trip.

Recent findings suggest that with that stated, I found the itinerary quite laid back. The amount of scheduled activities wasn’t overwhelming, and there was plenty of free time to do whatever you wanted. One couple I met even rented a car and explored Maui in their downtime, so they kept themselves busy.

These events are extremely popular, and many attendees I met at the Maui event had been on multiple Southwest cardmember trips.

Scoring a ticket to a Rapid Rewards Access Event might even require setting your alarm for when tickets drop. Several cardmembers told me they’ve experienced times when the event they wanted was sold out in hours, if not minutes. (The Maui one took a few hours to sell out, because it was larger than most.).

Finally, 275,000 points is a lot — even if you're getting great value. If your Rapid Rewards points are collecting dust in your account, then it could make sense. But if you have a transferable currency, then you'd have to weigh whether you might get better value elsewhere, such as booking round-trip business class flights.

Recent findings suggest that southwest isn’t the only airline or travel brand to offer special events for cardholders. United Airlines has MileagePlus Exclusives and United Card Events from Chase; Delta Air Lines offers cardmember-exclusive redemptions in its SkyMiles Experiences program; and Marriott has its Marriott Bonvoy Moments program.

According to recent reports, but every redemption option is different — even if it’s within the same loyalty program. For example, some Rapid Rewards Access Events are packages you can purchase immediately for a set price, while others are auction-style listings. Some programs offer paid experiences, so you can only pay in cash, not points.

Recent findings suggest that personally, I’m a fan of the fixed-price points option. You know the upfront price, and you don’t have to worry about getting into a last-minute bidding war that could lead you to paying more than you intended. Plus, Southwest has historically had limited award redemption options, although that will change in 2027 when it allows international partner award bookings.

Ultimately, whether you think a Rapid Rewards Access Event is a worthwhile redemption will depend on your interests, and Southwest is working to expand its offerings to meet people’s passions.

"We do offer a lot of breadth because we want to get different types of customers engaged with different types of things based on their individual passion points and what they're really interested in,” says Suri, the Rapid Rewards chief.

If you’d rather spend time in the mountains than on the beach, you might not want to spend 275,000 Rapid Rewards points on the Maui package.

Instead, you probably would've been interested in the 250,000-point package for "Boots, Bourbon and Bonfires" — a three-day trip to Devil's Thumb Ranch, an upscale dude ranch resort about 1.5 hours outside of Denver.

Before you book, just remember: You’ll need a Southwest credit card to purchase.

Signal to restrict screenshots over AI agent concerns – again

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set new limits on screenshots.
  • Whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers.
  • Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set new limits on screenshots. The manufacturer will prevent screenshotting in its iOS 27 app and “when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android,” Signal President Meredith Whittaker wrote in a blog post Friday.

Whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers. These features observe what’s on a user’s screen as context for completing requests.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why.

“Your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” Whittaker noted. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”.

Signal also blocked screenshots last year in response to Microsoft’s controversial Recall AI feature, which could capture screenshots of Signal chats on devices running Windows 11.

Signal’s move is another reminder of how Substantial Tech’s AI strategy trickles downstream. As AI features have moved from services external to the OS (like chatbots from OpenAI or Anthropic) to further inside of it, third-party apps have to adapt to conditions that undermine their hard-won privacy infrastructure.

Also: How I use Meta Muse safely to stretch my AI budget – and what I never let it do.

Sources indicate that just last week, researchers at Google DeepMind used AI agents to formally verify Signal’s code, building on Signal’s own work to essentially prove the app’s encryption works. That’s a high bar for a security guarantee within the app, but it becomes meaningless if an agent can simply grab messages off a screen.

Samsung is reportedly working on its own agent, Galaxy Claw, and Apple is developing a rival for Claude and ChatGPT as well.

Whittaker noted Signal’s screenshot restriction isn’t perfect, saying that AI agents can still access app data through other means, “such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.” Earlier this week, a Reuters investigation supported by Signal and the AI Now Institute found that Meta’s Muse AI agent was using permissions from its initial setup in unexpected ways to access apps and data that a user had not explicitly connected it to.

Signal noted its protections don’t at the moment work on MacOS.

According to recent reports, “It is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” she added. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience.”.

If you’d still like to take screenshots, you can simply disable the setting, though Signal’s announcement strongly advised against it.

“Doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees,” Whittaker mentioned.
